meaning.evidence: Every tactic and every protection survives, list for list: "Hang up, then ring the official number listed on the Login.gov or agency website.", "Always check the website URL ends in .gov." One shift: "Nine times outta ten they'll:" firms up "They often:" into a figure.

sense.evidence: "rorts goin' round", "fair dinkum", "suss profiles", "Want payin' on the spot" all carry the right sense. "Nine times outta ten" overstates "often" slightly.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a local explaining it: "Scammers never stop cookin' up brand-spankin'-new ways to con ya", "Fraudsters might give ya a ring makin' out they're from the government".

register.evidence: Full drawl and slang throughout, with swearing absent (allowed), but no asides beyond the original's points; a strong level 4 rather than a full yarn.

tone.evidence: The guide stays a practical warning: "Government agencies will never ask ya to pay over the phone."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly, lists stay parallel: "Get ya to log in with yer personal details" / "Charge ya fees for services that are free on the official sites".

variety.evidence: Good range, with "makin' out" ("Make out there's some urgent problem", "makin' out they're from the government", "makin' out they're government officials") and "dodgy" each used three times.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the Login.gov scam guide, headings and structure intact.

A.summary: Natural, faithful and fluent level-4 retelling of the guide.

meaning.evidence: Essentially the original text with a few swaps ("Scammers are constantly developing brand-spankin'-new methods"), so nearly everything survives; but "pressie cards" blurs the specific "gift cards" payment method.

sense.evidence: "Demand immediate payment via pressie cards" takes the wrong sense: gift cards are a specific payment product, and "pressie cards" reads as greeting cards.

authenticity.evidence: Slang bolted onto formal prose: "Scammers are constantly developing brand-spankin'-new methods to trick people", "double-check the spellin'" in an otherwise untouched sentence.

register.evidence: Largely untranslated: "Some scams use fraudulent websites designed to look like official government pages." is the original verbatim. Far off a level-5 brief.

tone.evidence: The original's advisory tone is untouched.

flow.evidence: Mostly the original's prose, so readable, but the bolted-on forms jar: "constantly developing brand-spankin'-new methods", "Avoid using search engines for sign in links—type the official URL directly and double-check the spellin'."

variety.evidence: Only g-drops and "yer" ("yer best defence", "protect yerself", "yer benefits") plus one swap.

essence.evidence: The guide's content is all there, but the stray dialect flattens it into neither the plain guide nor a retelling.

meaning.evidence: Every point kept: "Want payment on the spot by gift cards, cryptocurrency, or wire transfers", "Offer grants or financial help in return for fees up front".

sense.evidence: "rorts", "fair dinkum", "suss profiles", "gettin' in touch with the agency direct" fit exactly.

authenticity.evidence: Natural throughout: "Scammers are forever cookin' up brand-spankin'-new ways to con people", "Check the message is fair dinkum".

register.evidence: Drawl and slang throughout, but close to the original's sentence shapes ("Some scams use dodgy websites made to look like official government pages."); level 4 rather than 5.

tone.evidence: Practical warning intact: "Government agencies will never ask for payment over the phone."

flow.evidence: Smooth and parallel throughout: "Don't use search engines for sign in links—type the official URL in yerself and double-check the spellin'."

variety.evidence: Varied enough, with "dodgy" twice and "makin' out"/"Make out" twice.

problems.quote: Some scams use dodgy websites made to look like official government pages.
problems.original: Some scams use fraudulent websites designed to look like official government pages.
problems.why: Close to the original's wording; lighter than a level-5 yarn.

C.summary: Clean, accurate and natural; a restrained level-4 retelling.

meaning.evidence: All points survive, with elaborations that hang off them: "not whatever's in the message", "which is a dead giveaway right there", "cos one letter out is all it takes", "If one turns up, it's suss." "Nine times outta ten they'll:" overstates "often".

sense.evidence: "the grubs", "Looks the goods. Isn't.", "Spittin' image", "cough up some fees first" fit. "Ya knock one swifty on the head" blends two idioms (pull a swifty, knock on the head) but the sense comes through.

authenticity.evidence: Reads like a real Australian: "they've got another one goin' by smoko", "Charge ya fees for services that are free on the official sites, the cheek of it". "Strewth, where do I start?" is a slightly stock opener.

register.evidence: A full level-5 retelling with a narrator, linking openers ("First up,", "Then there's the phone.", "And last of all,") and asides, with no swearing past the dial ("the grubs").

tone.evidence: The warnings get firmer, not flippant: "Government agencies will never ask ya to pay over the phone. Never."

flow.evidence: Punchy and easy aloud; asides join cleanly ("Hurry ya along to click a link and “verify your account”, quick, before somethin' terrible happens").

variety.evidence: Wide range: "swifty", "smoko", "the goods", "Spittin' image", "the cheek of it", "cough up"; "suss" and "grubs" each appear twice.

essence.evidence: Every heading and list kept; unmistakably the guide, told as a yarn.

problems.quote: Ya knock one swifty on the head
problems.why: Blends "pull a swifty" with "knock on the head"; slightly off idiom.

D.summary: The best: a full, natural level-5 yarn whose asides sharpen the warnings without losing any point.

meaning.evidence: All tactics and protections kept: "Dob in dodgy messages to the agency", "Demand you pay up straight away with gift cards, crypto, or wire transfers". "paying up for stuff that's a total rort" recasts "making fraudulent payments" as paying for something overpriced.

sense.evidence: "Shonks", "Dob in", "Sting you with fees", "suss" fit. "Some scams use bodgy websites" takes the wrong sense (bodgy is shoddily made; these fakes are built to look official), and "Reckon there's some urgent drama" stretches reckon to mean claim.

authenticity.evidence: Natural idiom in standard spelling: "Shonks might ring up pretending to be from the government.", "Keeping your wits about you and knowing their tricks is your best defence."

register.evidence: Solid slang throughout, no drawl, no narrator; level 4 weight.

tone.evidence: Keeps the advisory tone: "Government agencies will never, ever ask you to pay over the phone."

flow.evidence: Reads cleanly, though "Dob in suss profiles on social media to the social media platform" keeps the original's repetition.

variety.evidence: Varied choices with little repeated: "dodges", "Hassle you", "Shonks", "Sting you", "bodgy", "Dob in".

essence.evidence: Still the guide, every section kept.

problems.why: Bodgy means shoddy; the point is that the fakes look official, so the term inverts the warning's sense.

problems.quote: paying up for stuff that's a total rort
problems.why: Shifts fraudulent payments toward overpriced purchases.

problems.original: Claim there is an urgent issue
problems.why: "reckon" is opinion, strained for a false claim.

E.summary: Varied, natural slang in a level-4 retelling, with one wrong-sense term ("bodgy").
